zh: 不同下标选出同一个字符序列只算一次，这是“不同子序列计数”问题；再叠加一个约束：从 x 出发，每一步都要停在 0..n 内并最终到达 y，空子序列在 x=y 时也算一个。
用 f[p] 表示已处理前缀能形成的、合法且终点为 p 的不同字符串个数。处理字符 c 时，在所有旧字符串后面接上 c，相当于把 f 整体平移一格（越界的部分丢掉）；但上一次处理同一个字母时追加出来的那批字符串会被再算一遍，需要减掉。
若 x 或 y 不在 0..n 内直接输出 0；否则令 f[x]=1，并为 l 和 r 各保存一份“上次追加量”数组。对每个字符先算出平移后的 added（r 取左边一格的 f，l 取右边一格的 f，越界处为 0），再令 f[p] 等于 f[p]+added[p] 减去该字母的上次追加量，最后用 added 替换该字母的上次追加量；每一步都取非负模，答案是 f[y]。
en: The same character sequence picked from different indices counts once, so this is a distinct-subsequence count with an extra constraint: starting at x, every step must stay within 0..n and the walk must end at y; the empty subsequence also counts when x = y.

Let f[p] be the number of distinct valid strings the processed prefix can form that end at p. Processing a character c appends c to every old string, which shifts f by one cell (dropping what falls off the line); but the strings appended the previous time the same letter was processed would be counted again and must be subtracted.

If x or y lies outside 0..n output 0; otherwise set f[x] = 1 and keep one last-added array for l and one for r. For each character compute the shifted array added (for r take f one cell to the left, for l one cell to the right, 0 off the line), set f[p] to f[p] + added[p] minus that letter's last-added value, then replace that letter's last-added array with added; keep every step a non-negative remainder, and the answer is f[y].

explanationEn:
## Fixed source, finite number line, and the empty subsequence

fastprep/Meesho/meesho-distinct-moves.md at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc states clearly: positions on the number line are 0..n, where n is the number line's upper bound; l turns j into j-1 and r turns j into j+1. Choose a subsequence of s and count the distinct character sequences that can walk from x to y, modulo 1000000007. The same string coming from different indices counts only once. The full ranges are 1<=|s|<=1000 and 0<=x,y,n<=2500, which must not be quietly narrowed to x,y<=n.

This site explicitly spells out what the finite number line means: the initial position of a path, every position along it, and its end must all belong to 0..n; a string that leaves the domain does not form a path on this number line. The rule is not reflection, staying put, or coming back after going out of bounds, because those would change the j+-1 transitions the original states explicitly. If, within the wide parameter ranges the original allows, x>n or y>n, the set of valid paths is empty and the result is 0; this is an explicit interpretation of the original domain, and it does not pretend that the original additionally guarantees x,y<=n.

The original says zero or more elements are deleted and does not require a non-empty result, so the empty subsequence obtained by deleting every character counts: when x=y and it lies in the domain, it contributes 1. When n=0 there is only position 0 and any non-empty move goes out of bounds, so the result is 1 for x=y=0 and 0 otherwise. s itself must still be non-empty; the lower bound on the input length cannot be changed to 0.

The original snapshot has no formal input/output examples. All three public examples were derived by this site: s=rr,n=2,x=0,y=1 counts the string r only once; s=lr,n=1,x=y=0 has only the empty string valid, because the first step of lr goes out of bounds; s=rl,n=1,x=y=0 has two, the empty string and rl. This site's input is s followed by n x y, and the output is an integer. The compiled code's ordinary choose/skip DP counts the same string from different indices repeatedly, for example getting 2 instead of 1 on the first example; the upstream code was not executed.

## Approach

f[p] counts the distinct strings the processed prefix can produce that start from x, always stay inside the domain, and end at p, including the empty string. The current character c has displacement +-1; shifting the old f gives added[p], and out-of-bounds contributions are not added. The new answer should be the old set united with all strings obtained by appending c, but strings that could already be produced the last time the same character was processed would be added again. Maintain last[c][p], the contribution recorded the last time c was appended, update f[p]=f[p]+added[p]-last[c][p], then set last[c]=added; take a non-negative remainder at every step.

## Proof of correctness

Initially there is only the empty string, which starts at a valid x and ends at x, so f[x]=1 is correct; an out-of-domain start or end can never form a path, so returning 0 directly is correct. Assume the old f represents exactly the set of distinct valid strings. Appending the current character is injective: different prefix strings stay different after appending the same letter; the same string has a unique movement trajectory and endpoint, so shifting the counts by the displacement and excluding out-of-bounds moves gives exactly the full set of newly appended strings.

If c has never appeared before, the appended set is disjoint from the old set. Otherwise, every string in the old set that ends with c can have its embedding end at the previous occurrence of c: the last c of its earlier embedding is no later than that position, and moving it to the previous c changes neither the character sequence nor the path. Therefore the intersection of the old set and the newly appended set is exactly the whole appended set recorded the last time c was processed. The set of the old prefix only grows, so the intersection is not undercounted; last[c] records the correct overlap per endpoint. Subtracting that intersection once gives the union with no omission and no duplication. By induction, the final f[y] is the answer.

## Complexity and full boundaries

Each character processes n+1 positions, so the time is O(|s|(n+1)) and the space O(n+1); the full 1000x2501 size runs directly. Counts can grow exponentially, so every state and every subtraction is normalized modulo 1000000007. Languages whose remainder can be negative must add the modulus. An out-of-bounds start or end must not be used directly as an array index.

## Independent verification

A small-domain brute force enumerates every selection mask, puts the resulting character sequences into a set to remove duplicates, simulates each path step by step, and checks the domain. It exhaustively covers every l/r string of length 1..7, n=0..3, and x/y=0..4, including out-of-domain endpoints, for 25400 cases in total.

The 163 oracle cases use an independent canonical-next DAG: from the remaining input, it separately picks the earliest l or the earliest r as the next character, and the recursion means continuing to count on the corresponding suffix; the same character sequence uses only its unique earliest embedding. Each state may additionally stop when the current position equals y, contributing 1 for the empty suffix. The implementation runs from right to left, keeps the successor rows of the two next-character branches, and does not use the reference's subtraction of the previous contribution. Short inputs are cross-checked against the mask-deduplication brute force, all large data use this independent DAG, and an unreduced big-integer DAG additionally checks the modular results.

The formal data cover the full |s|=1000 with n=2500, x/y=2500, out-of-domain starts and ends, n=0, the empty-string contribution, boundaries that cannot be crossed, deduplication of repeated characters, repeated alternation, several kinds of modular wraparound, and random cases. Two negative controls respectively skip subtracting the repeated contribution and wrongly exclude the empty string; all formal inputs must exit normally before a kill is counted.
